::: {.why}
The exponent decides your capacity, and getting it wrong in the optimistic direction is the single most common way a strategy that backtests well loses money at size.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the square-root impact law with its scaling arguments, and say what a linear model would predict differently at ten times the size.
- Implement an impact model with the exponent as an explicit parameter and report your strategy's cost under three values.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the Toth and co-authors paper's abstract, model section and main empirical figure. The claim is that impact scales as the square root of participation with a coefficient set by volatility, and the paper argues it follows from a condition on market liquidity rather than being an empirical accident.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Implement it in qlib/costs.py: impact in basis points equals a coefficient times volatility times participation raised to an exponent, with both coefficient and exponent as parameters rather than constants. Then report your two strategies' annual cost at exponents of 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 at a stated portfolio size.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note the parameter you cannot yet estimate: the coefficient. Week 43 fits it against real data. Until then it is an assumption and the milestone must say so.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Tóth et al. (2011) — Anomalous price impact and the critical nature of liquidity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.1694) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Almgren & Chriss (2000) — Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions](https://www.smallake.kr/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/optliq.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A parameterised impact model in qlib/costs.py, with annual cost reported at three exponents for both strategies.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Why is impact closer to the square root of size than to linear, and what does that do to your capacity estimate?
:::
